DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) approves an annual 
revenue requirement for The United Illuminating Company (UI or Company) in the amount 
of $450,789,348 for the rate year November 1, 2025, through October 31, 2026.  The 
Company may recover an additional $413,541 in executive compensation, provided the 
Company achieves certain performance targets.  The revenue requirement includes an 
allowed return on equity of 9.45%; however, the Authority reduces the allowed ROE by 
an aggregate 20 basis point reduction, to 9.25%, to address certain performance and 
management issues. 
In its application (Application), the Company proposed a 27.4% increase, or 
$105,418,797, over currently authorized revenues of $384,865,000, for a total revenue 
requirement of $490,283,797.  The Application included a 10.5% return on equity (ROE)—
a 140 basis point increase from the currently allowed 9.10% ROE. 1 
In addition to determining the revenue requirement, the Authority makes findings 
on a myriad of issues, including cost allocation and customer service. 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
UI is a public service company within the meaning of General Statutes § 16-1.  UI 
is a subsidiary of Avangrid Networks Inc. (Avangrid).  Hr’g Tr., 950:5–15. 2  The Company 
currently provides electric service to over 341,000 residential, commercial, and industrial 
customers in 17 towns and cities in the southwestern part of Connecticut. 
UI most recently increased its base distribution rates in 2023 by $22.957 million to 
$384.865 million.  22-08-08 Decision, p. 1.  UI appealed that decision in September 2023.  
On March 13, 2025, the Superior Court issued a memorandum of decision largely 
affirming the 22-08-08 Decision but remanding two minor items back for further 
proceedings. 
On July 9, 2025, the Authority issued a supplemental decision to address the two 
items on remand.  In the supplemental decision, the Authority increased UI’s approved 
annual revenue requirement by $165,000 to $385.030 million.

E. 
POSITION OF THE PARTIES AND INTERVENORS 
The Company seeks an increase in revenues of $105.4 million.  Application, p. 2.  
UI attributes the revenue deficiency to four categories of factors driving its request, 
including, alleged methodology deficiencies used to set base distribution rates in Docket 
No. 22-08-08, 5 costs that were not allowed to be recovered in Docket No. 22-08-08; 
increased inflationary costs related to labor, contracts, and distribution investments; and 
other factors affecting the Company’s operations, such as environmental remediation 
costs related to East Shore and changes in capital market conditions.  Id.  On October 
17, 2025, UI submitted a motion to adopt its “Alternative Resolution Position” (Motion No. 
120).  In Motion No. 120, the Company stated that a revenue increase of $63.7 million “is 
sufficient to enable the Company to operate its business and continue providing excellent 
service to its customers in Connecticut.”  Id., Ex. 1, p. 6.

residential customer and instead adopt OCC’s recommendations.  OCC Brief, p. 4.

English Station.  DEEP Brief, p. 1.  Further, DEEP recommends the Authority direct UI to

F. 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
The Authority held two in-person public comment hearings and one virtual public 
comment hearing.  UI presented a PowerPoint explaining its request at the start of each 
session before the admission of any public comment. 
The first in-person public comment hearing took place on January 27, 2025, at the 
Margaret Morton Government Center in Bridgeport, Connecticut, with approximately 30

the rate increase and one supporting the increase for infrastructure maintenance.  Public 
Hr’g Tr., Jan. 27, 2025, 14–24.  Fairfield representative and chair of the Committee on 
Energy Initiatives, John Kuhn, attended and expressed transparency concerns over the 
$286 million that UI has financed for plant additions as well as concerns over storm costs 
paid to out-of-state companies for line repairs.  Id., 23:11–19.  UI customers who spoke 
at the hearing expressed concerns regarding a myriad of topics, including: the 
environmental impact on delivery; the difficulties an increase would cause seniors with

At the virtual comment hearing on March 18, 2025, eight individuals were in

letters and emails in opposition were the negative financial impact on customers, 
particularly senior citizens, and low-income families.  Given the current cost of living and 
inflation, the requested increase would place additional financial strain on customers.  
Senator Jason D. Perillo submitted his concerns regarding the impact a rate increase will 
have on households and businesses and urged the Authority to prioritize the interests of 
the ratepayers.  Perillo Corresp., Mar. 13, 2025.  Senator Perillo recognizes the 
importance of grid investments; however, UI customers have endured a 32% rate 
increase since January of 2019, which is unreasonable to residents struggling with

Ganim Corresp., Oct. 21, 2024.  The mayor stated many residents are spending over 
50% of their income on housing security and an additional 9% rate increase would be

II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
The Authority is statutorily charged with regulating the rates of Connecticut’s public 
service companies.  General Statutes § 16-19.  The term “public service company” is 
defined to include electric distribution companies, such as UI.  See General Statutes § 
16-1.  Consequently, UI must “file any proposed amendment of its existing rates with the 
[A]uthority in such form and in accordance with such reasonable regulations as the 
[A]uthority may prescribe.” 8  General Statutes § 16-19(a).  Once a proposed rate 
amendment has been filed, the Authority is responsible for making “such investigation of 
such proposed amendment of rates as is necessary to determine whether such rates 
conform to the principles and guidelines” in General Statutes § 16-19e, and the Authority 
must investigate whether the rates “are unreasonably discriminatory or more or less than 
just, reasonable and adequate, or that the service furnished by such company is 
inadequate to or in excess of public necessity and convenience . . . .”  General Statutes 
§ 16-19(a). 
Importantly, a public service company bears “the burden of proving the proposed 
rate under consideration is just and reasonable.”  General Statutes § 16-22.  In placing 
the burden on the company in rate cases, the General Assembly has attempted to remedy 
a critical challenge in setting rates — asymmetric access to information.  The utility 
maintains most of the relevant and critical information necessary for the Authority to make 
findings of fact and associated determinations on rates.  Therefore, the Authority and 
other parties are at an information disadvantage compared to the utility and must rely on 
the utility’s application materials, the utility’s responses to interrogatories, and the utility’s 
witness testimony.  Accordingly, the burden of proof established by General Statutes § 
 
8  Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-1-53 et seq. apply to rate amendment applications.

Docket No. 24-10-04 
 
Page 8 
 
16-22 addresses the information imbalance by imposing an affirmative obligation on the 
utility to present sufficient evidence to support its proposed rate amendment. 
In administrative proceedings, which are subject to the provisions of the Uniform 
Administrative Procedures Act (UAPA), General Statutes § 4-166 et seq., the appropriate 
standard of proof is the preponderance of the evidence.  See Jones v. Connecticut 
Medical Examining Board, 309 Conn. 727, 734–35, 741 n.7 (2013) (“default rule is the 
preponderance of the evidence standard in the absence of legislation to the contrary”); 
Goldstar Medical Services, Inc. v. Dept. of Social Services, 288 Conn. 790, 821 (2008) 
(same).  “That burden of proof is met when [the company] shows the facts supporting [its] 
case are found to be more probable than not.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. 
Connecticut Dept. of Public Utility Control, No. CV094019951S, 2010 WL 797137, at *10 
(Conn. Super. Ct. Feb. 5, 2010) (citing Tianti v. William Raveis Real Estate, Inc., 231 
Conn. 690, 702 (1995)).  Consequently, to carry its statutory burden, the utility must 
provide (or ensure the record contains) evidence that, inter alia, the requested rates are 
consistent with the principles that rates be “sufficient, but no more than sufficient,” General 
Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4), and “reflect prudent and efficient management.”  General 
Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5). 
Notably, the utility bears the burden of providing more than mere declarations of 
fact.  Connecticut Natural Gas Corp. v. Public Utilities Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. 379, 
394 (1971) (finding “no sacrosanctity about the testimony of any company officer 
regardless of his position which gives such testimony any godlike fiat that must be 
accepted out of hand” by the Authority).  “Bald statements need to be covered with some 
evidential hair” before they are acceptable.  Id.  Further, “[a]n administrative agency is not 
required to believe any witness, even an expert.”  Goldstar, 288 Conn. at 830.  It is the 
province of the trier of fact, in this case, the Authority, to “make determinations of 
credibility, crediting some, all, or none of a given witness’ testimony.”  Id. 
The Authority’s review of the proposed rates is guided, in part, by the principle “that 
the level and structure of rates be sufficient, but no more than sufficient, to allow public 
service companies to cover their operating and capital costs, to attract needed capital 
and to maintain their financial integrity, and yet provide appropriate protection to the 
relevant public interests, both existing and foreseeable.”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  
That language “tracks, almost verbatim, the language that the United States Supreme 
Court used in Hope when it interpreted the ‘just and reasonable’ requirement under the 
Natural Gas Act and the federal constitution.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of 
Public Utility Control, 216 Conn. 627, 635 (1990) (referencing Federal Power Commission 
v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591, 603 (1944)).  A regulated utility is entitled to an 
opportunity to recover prudent operating expenses as well as capital costs, including a 
fair and reasonable rate of return on capital investments.  See Hope, 320 U.S. at 603; 
Bluefield Waterworks & Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 
262 U.S. 679, 690 (1923) (company entitled to ask for fair return upon value of capital 
employed for public convenience); see also Duquesne Light Co. v. Barasch, 488 U.S. 
299, 310 (1989) (affirming the holding in Hope that “[i]f the total effect of the rate order 
cannot be said to be unreasonable, judicial inquiry . . . is at an end.”).  “The prudence of 
a management decision depends on good faith and reasonableness, judged at the time

Docket No. 24-10-04 
 
Page 9 
 
the decision is made.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public Utility Control, 
216 Conn. at 645. 
Ultimately, however, rate setting requires “a balancing of the investor and 
consumer interests.”  Woodbury Water Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 174 Conn. 258, 
264 (1978) (quoting Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. at 
603).  Further, the constitution does not bind the Authority “to the use of any single formula 
or combination of formulae in determining rates,” and the ratemaking process may involve 
“pragmatic adjustments.”  Woodbury Water Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 174 Conn. 
at 264 (1978) (quoting Federal Power Commission v. Natural Gas Pipeline Co., 315 U.S. 
575, 586 (1942)).  In striking this balance and making pragmatic adjustments, the 
Authority is guided by the principles of General Statutes § 16-19e(a), noted above. 
III. 
TEST YEAR 
A test year “is employed to show what the probable operating and financial 
condition of the company will be in the immediate future, in order that rates may be fixed 
which will compensate the company for all operating expenses and provide it with a fair 
return.”  Southern New England Telephone Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 29 Conn. 
Supp. 253, 258 (1970).  The test year in each rate application must “consist of the most 
recent twelve-month period available ending at a calendar quarter.”  Conn. Agencies 
Regs. § 16-1-54.  Test year financial data is “limited to the actual income and expenses 
as determined on the accrual basis during the subject period without adjustment or 
alteration.”  Id.  Applicants are required to present financial data through the SFRs.  See 
Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-1-53. 
Here, UI proposed the period beginning January 1, 2023, and ending December 
31, 2023, as the test year (Test Year).  Application, p. 2. 
IV. 
RATE BASE 
A. 
SUMMARY 
Rate base is a fundamental concept of cost-of-service ratemaking.  Rate base is 
the investor-supplied facilities and other investments necessary to supply a utility service 
to consumers in a safe, reliable, and cost-effective manner.  For ratemaking, rate base is 
the capital on which the investor may earn a return.  See Federal Power Commission v. 
Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. at 596 (rate base calculated from “‘actual legitimate cost’ 
of the company's interstate property less depletion and depreciation and plus unoperated 
acreage, working capital and future net capital additions”).  A “company is entitled to ask 
[for] a fair return upon the value of that which it employs for the public convenience.”  
Bluefield Waterworks & Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 
262 U.S. at 690. 
Cost-of-service ratemaking provides a return on rate base, which is the capital that 
has been prudently invested by shareholders and put to public use.  Id.  Consequently, 
determining rate base requires a two-prong assessment.  First, the utility must prove that 
the company’s plant is in use and is serving the public.  See Cedar Island Improvement

Docket No. 24-10-04 
 
Page 10 
 
Association. v. Clinton Electric Light & Power Co., 142 Conn. 359, 370 (1955) (“public 
utility company is entitled to a fair return upon the fair value of such of its property as is 
useful and being used in providing service”).  Second, the company must prove that the 
capital investment was prudent and reasonable.  See General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5) 
(“the level and structure of rates charged customers shall reflect prudent and efficient 
management”). 
The “used and useful” standard is a “bedrock principle of utility regulation.”  
Kentucky Utilities Co. v. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 760 F.2d 1321, 1324 
n.4 (D.C. Cir. 1985).  “Generally speaking, property not employed in the public service 
should not be incorporated into the base to be used to compute the fair rate of return . . . 
whether utility property is used or useful for inclusion in the rate base is a factual 
determination rather than a legal question.”  Southern New England Telephone Co. v. 
Public Utilities Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. 253, 259–60 (1970).  The Authority does not 
allow for the inclusion of incomplete system additions or improvements into a company’s 
pro forma rate base.  See, e.g., Decision, May 19, 2021, Docket No. 20-10-31, Application 
of Jewett City Water Company to Amend its Rate Schedules, pp. 23–24 (“ratepayers 
benefit from the plant additions when they are in-service and . . . ratepayers should not 
be responsible for providing a return on plant that is not in-service”). 
Once a company has proven that property is used and useful, the company must 
also establish that the capital investment was prudent and reasonable.  See General 
Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5).  Specifically, “there exists a distinction between, on one hand, 
utility property and, on the other hand, the cost of utility property allowed in rate base, 
because only that portion of utility property that is the result of prudent and reasonable 
management is included in rate base.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public 
Utility Control, 219 Conn. 61, 68 (1991).  To demonstrate prudency, the utility must provide 
evidence that the decision to undertake the investment was reasonable at the time it was 
made and that the capital project was managed in a reasonable and cost-effective 
manner.  In sum, to establish its rate base for ratemaking purposes, the company must 
demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the capital proposed for inclusion 
in rate base (1) is used and useful and (2) was invested prudently. 
Rate base is calculated by taking the test year net book value of prudent capital 
investments and accounting for other factors, including accumulated depreciation, 
working capital, and non-rate base capital such as deferred taxes.  The test year is 
intended to “be representative of conditions which will probably prevail in the immediate 
future when the rates will be effective.”  Connecticut Natural Gas Corp. v. Public Utilities 
Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. at 390.  Certain pro forma adjustments may be permitted 
to recognize capital investments and other changes to rate base that occur after the test 
year.  Id., p. 390 (“company should be permitted to adjust the test year forward for a 
reasonable period of time where definitely ascertainable expenses are involved during 
such future period”).

To investigate the reasonableness of the capital additions proposed by UI, PURA 
Staff conducted an engineering and accounting audit at the Company’s headquarters.

$2,273,831,000 plant-in-service balance from the Company’s previous rate case with the 
$2,739,061,244 plant-in-service Rate Year ending balance that the Company proposed

retirements.  22-08-08 Decision, p. 13; Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2, Sch. B-2.0.  The Authority

orders and vendor invoices, of the Company supporting new plant additions placed in-
service between September 1, 2022, and December 31, 2024.  See PURA Corresp., Jan. 
28, 2025.  PURA Staff reviewed those records to ensure that all incremental capital 
investments being sought for recovery in rate base were fully disclosed and accounted

Accumulated depreciation (or depreciation reserve) reflects the amount of 
depreciation expense that has been allowed in rates and accumulated to date, less any 
retirements and net salvage received as an offset to rate base.  See 22-08-08 Decision, 
p. 20; Decision, July 28, 2021, Docket No. 20-12-30, Application of the Connecticut Water 
Company to Amend its Rate Schedule (20-12-30 Decision), p. 70.  As such, the 
depreciation reserve reflects the asset deterioration of in-service plant and is maintained 
in anticipation of future asset replacement or retirement needs.  Id.  The accumulated 
depreciation should be based on the depreciation rates and useful service lives that fall 
within the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC) guidelines 
and have been allowed or approved by the Authority.  Id.  Ideally, assets are depreciated 
consistently, i.e., proportionally, with the rate of the actual deterioration of assets until they 
are retired or replaced.  Id. 
The product of the depreciation rate and plant-in-service balance is the annual 
depreciation expense, which is recorded to reflect the annual recovery or amortization of 
previously expended capital investment.  The depreciation expense impacts the 
calculation of accumulated depreciation as any depreciation expense allowed for in rates, 
past or current, should be accounted for in some way in the calculation of accumulated 
depreciation.  Section VI.B, Depreciation Expense, below, details the Authority’s analysis 
of the allowed annual depreciation expense of $84,026,124, which is $2,923,090 less 
than UI’s proposed depreciation expense. 
The Authority may calculate the depreciation reserve to include all depreciation 
that occurs through the beginning of the Rate Year (i.e., November 1, 2025), because the 
Company’s rate base does not cease depreciating at the close of the evidentiary record.  
See Aquarion Water Company of Connecticut v. Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, No. 
HHB-CV-23-6078177-S, 2024 WL 1403433, at *9 (Conn. Super. Ct. Mar. 25, 2024) 
(holding a utility’s “rate base does not somehow cease depreciating after [a date following 
which the utility] failed to present sufficient evidence demonstrating that capital 
investments made by [the utility] after that date were reasonable and prudent.  
Depreciation continues to occur regardless, even if [the utility] fails to meet its evidentiary 
burden as necessary to enter investments into rate base.”).  Nonetheless, after examining 
the specific facts of the instant proceeding, the Authority exercises its discretion regarding 
the accumulated depreciation accrual date in recognition of the statutory obligation to set 
just and reasonable rates while “faced with varied and complex accounting procedures 
when considering rate increase applications.”  See Aquarion Water Company of 
Connecticut v. Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, No. HHB-CV-23-6078177-S, 2024 WL 
1403433, at *9 (Conn. Super. Ct. Mar. 25, 2024) (quoting Woodbury Water Co., 174 Conn. 
at 266).  The Authority “must remain flexible in order to meet its overall obligation of setting 
just and reasonable rates that balance the interests of the consumer as well as that of the 
company.”  Woodbury Water Co., 174 Conn. at 267.  Accordingly, the Authority elects not 
to include the accumulated depreciation of $37,029,884 for the period May 1, 2025, 
through October 31, 2025, based on the Authority’s allowed plant-in-service, for purposes 
of calculating rate base in this proceeding.

It is a customary regulatory practice to include a CWC allowance – an adjustment 
to rate base in recognition of the timing difference between when revenues are received 
and when expenses are paid.  For larger utilities, the Authority has established a 
preference that a lead-lag study be conducted to determine the appropriate CWC 
allowance, rather than to rely on a heuristic approach (such as a percentage of an 
operation and maintenance (O&M) expense). 
There is a myriad of issues present with respect to UI’s proposal for its cash 
working capital allowance.  First, the Company’s proposed cash working capital 
calculation is inconsistent with the calculation methodology approved by the Authority in 
Docket No. 23-11-02.  23-11-02 CNG Decision, pp. 24–28.  The Company’s calculation 
methodology includes non-cash items that were explicitly not allowed in the prior case by 
the Authority.  23-11-02 CNG Decision, pp. 25–26.  In addition, the Collection Lag for the 
Test Year in this proceeding is 2.41 days shorter than the Collection Lag for 2021.  
Interrog. Resp. RSR-267.  Using the Collection Lag for 2021 improperly inflated the 
Company’s CWC request by $1,769,819.  Finally, the Company utilized an unsupported 
Payment Lag.  The Company’s inclusion of the unsupported Payment Lag inflated the 
Company’s CWC request by $734,365. 
b. Lead/Lag Study 
For purposes of calculating its proposed cash working capital allowance in the 
instant proceeding, UI relied on a lead-lag study that was originally developed for Docket

No. 22-08-08.  This study detailed the lead/lag period to expenses and revenues.  The 
“lag” is measured in days and represents the time between when customers receive 
service and the date customers’ payments are received.  These “lag” days are offset by 
“lead” days, which represent the time between when a Company receives goods and 
services and when it pays for them.  22-08-08 Decision, pp. 22–23. 
i. 
Non-cash Items 
In its calculation of CWC, the Company included non-cash items, such as 
depreciation, amortization expense, and deferred taxes.  Ex. UI-RRP-1, pp. 123–124.  
OCC argued that non-cash expenses should not be part of the calculation of CWC.  
Defever PFT, p. 5. 
In support of its inclusion of non-cash items, the Company argues that there are 
two “broad approaches to performing lead-lag studies.”  Ex. UI-RRP-1, p. 120.  The 
Company refers to one methodology as the “O&M approach” (Approach 1), which does 
not include non-cash items, and focuses “on O&M cash expenses, plus taxes.”  Ex. UI-
RRP-1, p. 120.  The Company refers to the other methodology as the “non-O&M 
approach” (Approach 2), which uses all cash flows but also incorporates “items that are 
considered ‘non-cash’ from an accounting definition” but that UI claims have “cash-flow 
implications for the Company.”  Ex. UI-RRP-1, p. 120.  The Company proposes to use 
this second methodology.  Ex. UI-RRP-1, pp. 125–126.  Although the Company proposes 
Approach 2, it claims that “[i]f utilized correctly, either method will produce a reasonable 
estimate of cash working capital requirements, and regulators in various jurisdictions have 
relied on both methods.”  Ex. UI-RRP-1, p. 120. 
Based on the evidence in the record, the Authority finds that Approach 1 is the 
more appropriate methodology by which to calculate CWC and, therefore, does not allow 
the inclusion of non-cash items in the CWC calculation.  Notably, the Company’s own 
definition of CWC does not allow for the inclusion of non-cash items in CWC.  22-08-08 
Decision, p. 22 ("[CWC is] the amount of funds required to be kept on hand to finance the 
day-to-day operations of the Company.”).  Because CWC is fundamentally cash-based, 
inclusion of non-cash data is incompatible with its purpose. 
Additionally, the Company’s claim that Approach 1 and Approach 2 both produce 
a “reasonable estimate” of CWC is not supported by the evidence in the record.  The 
Company’s own analysis found that the Company’s preferred approach (Approach 2) 
resulted in CWC that is over $12 million higher than when calculating with Approach 1.  
Late Filed Ex. 1, Sch. B-4.0 WP ($38.981 million vs. $26.963 million). 
For the foregoing reasons, the Authority approves the use of Approach 1, which 
removes uncollectibles, depreciation, amortization, deferred taxes, interest, net income – 
external dividend, and net income – retained, from the CWC calculation.  The exclusion 
of all non-cash items results in a CWC that is $12,018,421 less than that proposed by UI.

ii. Collections Lag 
The Collections Lag is a component of the Company’s proposed revenue lag 
computation.  Interrog. Resp. RSR-266, Att. 1.  In the instant proceeding, the Company 
proposes the same collections lag of 44.27 days that it used in Docket No. 22-08-08.  Ex. 
UI-RRP-1, p. 119.  Calendar year 2021 data was used to calculate the proposed 
collections lag.  Interrog. Resp. RSR-267. 
When asked in discovery whether the Company conducted any analysis to 
determine whether the proposed collection lag remains appropriate, the Company stated 
that it did not perform such analysis, but that reliance on a lead-lag study for multiple year 
periods is consistent with prior cases.  Interrog. Resp. RSR-267.  The Company also 
asserted that the calculated collections lag is similar to the amounts accepted in previous 
proceedings (specifically, Docket Nos. 13-01-19 and 16-06-04) and that using the 2021 
financial data “has the further benefit of being calculated over a period consistent with the 
period over which expense leads were calculated.”  Interrog. Resp. RSR-267. 
The Company’s reliance on seven- to ten-year-old rate case data is unpersuasive, 
as such data points provide little—if any—meaningful information in this particular 
instance.  Additionally, evidence in the record demonstrates that, when the Test Year data 
for the instant proceeding (2023) is used to calculate the collections data, the results are 
significantly different than the Company’s proposed collections lag.  The Company’s 
proposed collections lag (using 2021 data) is 44.27 days, whereas the collections lag 
using 2023 data is 41.86 days, a reduction of 2.41 days.  Interrog. Resp. RSR-267.  The 
Authority also does not find compelling the Company’s claim that there is a “benefit” to 
the 2021 data being used because the data is “consistent with the period over which 
expense leads were calculated.”  The Company could have chosen to update all elements 
of its lead-lag study with 2023 data if it had deemed such a factor to be important.  The 
fact that it chose not to does not preclude the Authority, where supported by the record, 
from adjusting individual components of the lead-lag study to be more reflective of current 
data.  Accordingly, the Authority adopts a collections lag of 41.86 days based on 2023 
data, reducing the Company’s proposed lag by 2.41 days and lowering CWC by 
$1,769,819. 
iii. Payment Lag 
Similar to the Collections Lag, the payment processing lag is a component of the 
Company’s proposed revenue lag computation.  Interrog. Resp. RSR-266, Att. 1.  For 
purposes of the Company’s calculation, UI assumed a payment lag of one day.  Interrog. 
Resp. RSR-266, Att. 1.  The Company’s assumption of a one-day lag lacks evidentiary 
support.  Specifically, the spreadsheet provided as support for this figure contained a 
hard-coded “1” in the column titled “Average Lag Time Days” with no underlying 
calculation for how the “1” was derived.  Interrog. Resp. RSR-269, Att. 1. 
The Company also made assumptions in its calculations that appear inconsistent 
with the underlying data.  For example, the Company used a one-day payment lag for 
“Wires/ACH” payments, even though the description of this item states that these 
payments are processed “same-day.”  Interrog. Resp. RSR-269, Att. 2.

UI’s Reliability Plan complies with the Reliability Framework requirements

Framework outlined planning parameters that should enable UI to maintain top quartile 
reliability, while also improving upon it when necessary or cost-effective to do so.  Id., p. 
43.  Multi-year reliability investment plans must include an analysis that targets a 5% blue-
sky reliability improvement over prior four year-average reliability improvement.  Id., p. 
44.  The 5% improvement is a planning parameter, not a standard.  Id. 
The plan may depend also on (1) whether the Company achieved top-quartile

reliability category spending and then escalating those costs by the GDP Deflator index

reliability investment plan exceeds the affordability analysis, then UI must include some 
reliability improvement target for the incremental spend.  Id., p. 46.  If the proposed budget 
is under the threshold, UI may target a 0% reliability improvement.  Id.  UI may also 
propose a different affordability definition (i.e., threshold analysis).  Id. 
First, UI has achieved top-quartile reliability performance as measured by both

thresholds articulated in General Statutes § 16-244i(d) from 2014-2023 with two 
exceptions.  In 2014 and in 2018, UI exceeded the General Statutes § 16-244i(d) 
threshold for SAIDI.  All other years were under the threshold for both SAIDI and SAIFI.  
When looking at the four-year rolling average, UI did not exceed the threshold for SAIDI 
or SAIFI.  Interrog. Resp. RSR-191, Att. 1.

exceed the 10-year inflation-adjusted (using GDP Deflator index) historical capital spend 
for reliability programs.  Ex. UI-CIP-9, p. 10.  UI’s Capital Plan breaks investments down

Although UI’s affordability analysis in the application uses the GDP Deflator index 
to normalize costs, UI proposes that the Handy-Whitman (HW) Index is a better measure 
to reflect costs experienced by a utility over time.  The choice of index does not have a 
material effect on this Application, as the proposed CapEx is under the affordability 
threshold using the GDP Deflator Index.  However, the Authority notes that the HW Index 
is typically a better reflection of utility costs.  The GDP deflator is a formula that measures 
the real value of the U.S. economy’s total output reduced by inflation over time and, 
therefore, measures the change in costs over time based on the entire U.S. economy and 
is reflective of how costs impact consumers.  See Ex. UI-CIP-9, p. 35.  The Handy-
Whitman Index reflects escalation of utility costs over time and has an index specific to 
northeast utilities (rather than the entire country, as the GDP Deflator Index reflects).  Id.  
Specifically, the GDP Deflator Index considers economy-wide measures such as personal 
consumption expenditures, private domestic investment, exports of goods and services, 
and government expenditures and consumption.  Ex. UI-CIP-9, p. 36.  By contrast, the 
HW Index considers utility construction costs by FERC plant account (e.g., transformers, 
meters, overhead conductors, station equipment).  Id.  The HW Index better reflects costs 
of utilities doing business, while the GDP Deflator reflects costs from the consumer’s 
perspective.  Cost escalation according to the HW Index has outpaced that of the GDP 
Inflator, particularly since 2021/2022.  Ex. UI-CIP-9, p. 37.  As of 2024, the GDP Deflator-
measured inflation was 5% since 2022 (13% since 2021) and the HW Index-measured 
inflation was 35% since 2022 (49% since 2021).  Ex. UI-CIP-9, p. 37.  Key contributors to 
the significant escalation rates of the HW Index since 2021 have been for major 
distribution equipment: transformers, overhead and underground conductors, and meters 
(though not as significant as the other contributors).  See Interrog. Resp. OCC-374, Att. 
1, p. 2.

UI’s Resilience Plan complies with the Resilience Framework requirements

resilience measures are evaluated and selected for each identified zone.  Id., p. 62.  There

3. Capital Structure Analysis 
The Authority establishes the ratemaking capital structure by carefully weighing 
several factors, including: the actual capital structure of the utility and its parent company; 
the range of capital structures of the proxy group; and the credit rating agency metrics.  
The Authority is obligated to balance both investor and consumer interests in reaching a 
determination on the appropriate capital structure.  Woodbury Water Co., 174 Conn. At 
264.  Generally, the utility will advocate for a higher equity component in its capital 
structure because a higher equity component generally provides a higher return for its 
investors.  At the same time, a higher equity component also decreases the financial risk 
of the Company as it holds less debt in its capital structure.  Conversely, parties such as

Docket No. 24-10-04

OCC will often advocate for a lower equity component in the Company’s capitalization 
structure because debt is generally less expensive for ratepayers than equity. 
Nonetheless, investor and consumer interests in capital structure are not entirely 
divergent.  Specifically, a capital structure with too little equity could maximize the benefits 
of lower cost debt but would ultimately increase the Company’s risk profile and, therefore, 
the cost of equity.  On the other hand, a capital structure with too much equity would 
unnecessarily burden ratepayers with a more expensive capital structure and not achieve 
the lowest cost of capital for the Company that balances both risk and the overall cost of 
capital.  Consequently, the Authority must account for a variety of factors to find an optimal 
capitalization mix for the Company’s cost of capital. 
a. Approved and Actual Capital Structure 
The first factor to consider when determining a reasonable capital structure for 
ratemaking purposes is the approved and actual capital structure of the Company.  In 
both the February 4, 2009, Decision in Docket No. 08-07-04, Application of The United 
Illuminating Company to Increase its Rates and Charges (08-07-04 Decision), and the 
13-01-19 Decision, the Company proposed, and the Authority approved, a capital 
structure of 50% common equity and 50% long-term debt.  08-07-04 Decision, pp. 6, 139; 
13-01-19 Decision, pp. 86, 95.  In both the December 14, 2016 Decision in Docket No. 
16-06-04, Application of The United Illuminating Company to Increase its Rates and 
Charges (16-06-04 Decision) and the 22-08-08 Decision, the Company proposed a

and 50% long-term debt.  16-06-04 Decision, pp. 60, 63; 22-08-08 Decision, p. 63.  Said 
another way, while the Company has proposed progressively higher equity capitalization

The Company’s average Debt to Equity capitalization from January 2022 to

2. Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) Model 
a. DCF Model Description 
The DCF model is a market-based financial model that attempts to replicate the 
valuation process used by investors.  The DCF model assumes that investors evaluate 
stocks in a classical economic framework and buy and sell securities rationally at prices 
that reflect the assets’ value.  Under the DCF model, the value of a financial asset is 
based upon the present value principle.  Specifically, the present value of a financial asset 
equals the discounted value of its expected future cash flow.  Investors discount these 
expected cash flows at their required rate of return (i.e., the COE or ROE).  Therefore, by 
using proxy company data, the DCF model provides evidence of commensurate ROEs 
for utilities with corresponding risk profiles. 
The traditional constant growth DCF Model requires the following assumptions: a 
constant growth rate for earnings and dividends; a stable dividend payout ratio; a constant 
price-to-earnings ratio; and a discount rate greater than the expected growth rate. 
The DCF model is represented by the formula of K = D1 / Po + G, where: 
K = the market-required ROE 
D1 = the forecasted dividend paid one period into the future; 
Po = an estimate of the current market price of the stock; and 
G = investors’ long-run growth expectations. 
In short, the ROE (K) can be determined by summing the expected dividend yield 
(D1/Po) and the expected growth rate (G). 
b. Expected Growth Rate 
The Authority first considers the expected growth rate for the companies in the 
Authority Proxy Group because the expected growth rate is also a factor in calculating 
the expected dividend yield.  The constant growth form of the DCF Model assumes a 
single growth estimate in perpetuity.  To reduce the expected growth rate to a single 
measure, the constant payout ratio, earnings per share (EPS), dividends per share (DPS), 
and book value per share (BVPS) are assumed to all grow at the same constant rate.  
The distinction between the Parties’ approaches to the expected growth rate is (1) the 
specific growth measures considered and (2) the weighting of the measures.

c. Expected Dividend Yield 
The second input into the DCF model is the Expected Dividend Yield.  For 
purposes of the DCF model, the Expected Dividend Yield is estimated by taking a 
company’s current annual dividend yield and escalating the yield to account for 
anticipated growth and the timing of dividends. 
A company’s current dividend yield is not subject to much dispute since a 
company’s dividend and stock price are both published market data.  To avoid stock price 
fluctuations, an average daily stock price is typically used, with the time period ranging 
from 30 to 180 trading days.  Here, as has been found in other recent rate cases, the

represents the most current pricing data over a reasonable duration of time and does not

3. Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) 
a. CAPM Model Description 
The CAPM evaluates the relationship between the expected return and risk of 
investing in a security; CAPM can be used to calculate the expected return of an asset.  
Therefore, like the DCF model, by incorporating proxy company data, the CAPM provides 
evidence of commensurate ROEs for utilities with corresponding risk profiles. 
To determine the COE, the CAPM first determines the appropriate risk-free rate 
and then adds a beta, or the degree of co-movement of the security’s rate of return with 
the market’s rate of return, multiplied by the expected equity risk premium (ERP), which 
is the amount by which investors expect the future return on equities, in general, to exceed 
that on the risk-free asset. 
The CAPM model is represented by the formula Ke = Rf + β (Rm-Rf), where: 
Ke= the required market ROE; 
β = Beta coefficient of an individual security; 
Rf = the risk-free rate of return; and 
Rm = the required return on the market; the term (Rm - Rf) represents the ERP. 
Consequently, once the Beta (β) and ERP (Rm- Rf) are determined, an ROE can 
be calculated.

d. Equity Risk Premium 
The equity risk premium (ERP) is equal to the expected return on the S&P 500 
(Rm) minus the risk-free rate of interest (Rf).  In short, ERP = Rm-Rf.  The ERP is difficult 
to measure because it requires an estimate of the expected return on the market (Rm). 
The Company defined the market risk premium as the difference between the 
implied expected equity market return and the risk-free rate.  Ex. UI-AEB-1, p. 30.  The 
Company calculated the expected return on the S&P 500 Index by using the constant 
growth DCF model for the companies in the S&P 500 Index.  Id.; Application, Ex. UI-AEB-
7.  The Company’s estimated required market return for the S&P 500 Index, as of 
September 30, 2024, is 12.04%, based on an estimated market capitalization weighted 
dividend yield of 1.52% and a weighted long-term growth rate of 10.45%.  Ex. UI-AEB-1, 
p. 42; Application, Ex. UI-AEB-7.  The Company then determined an ERP (Rm-Rf) by 
using three estimates of the risk-free rate, the current 30-day average of 30-year T-Bond 
(4.07%), the average projected 30-year U.S Treasury bond yield for the first quarter of 
2025 through the first quarter of 2026 (4.02%), and the average projected 30-year U.S. 
Treasury bond yield for 2026 through 2030 (4.30%), resulting in a market risk premium 
range of 7.74% to 8.02%.  Ex. UI-AEB-1, pp. 29–30. 
On rebuttal, the Company updated its ERP to a range of 8.58% to 8.75%.  Bulkley 
Rebuttal PFT, UI-AEB-Rebuttal-4B.

historical risk premium (i.e., ex-post returns); (2) ex-ante market risk premium studies; (3)

beta coefficient and market risk premium by applying a weight of 0.25 to the market risk 
premium and 0.75 to the beta.  Ex. UI-AEB-1, pp. 31–32.  The Company’s ECAPM 
formula is represented by:

OCC indicated that the ECAPM has not been theoretically or empirically validated 
in journals.  Woolridge PFT, p. 73.  Beyond the lack of validation, OCC states that the 
Company’s ECAPM has two main flaws: (1) there are no known tests of the CAPM that 
use adjusted betas as posed by the Company; and (2) adjusted betas address the 
empirical issues with CAPM.  Id. 
The Authority has previously reviewed the ECAPM approach and excluded this 
method.  See, e.g., 22-08-08 Decision, pp. 84–85; 23-08-32 Decision, p. 57; 23-11-02 
CNG Decision, p. 79.  Here, the Authority reviewed the proposed ECAPM and sees no 
difference from past submissions.  The most recent rationale for rejection of the ECAPM 
holds true today: the Authority believes that the 0.75/.25 factor is out-of-date (based on 
30 plus year old data) and incorporates another level of conjecture that is unnecessary 
given that the simple CAPM formula is widely accepted in cost of equity literature.  
Second, given that ECAPM is only discussed within the regulatory cost of capital sphere, 
ECAPM has not been theoretically or empirically validated in financial journals.  Third, the 
purpose of adjusted betas such as those from Value Line and Bloomberg address the 
empirical issues with the CAPM.  Hence, there is no need for an additional adjustment 
factor to adjust for what is being addressed by using Value Line and Bloomberg betas.  
Interrog. Resp. RRU-167; Interrog. Resp. RRU-169.

results as its main purpose is to artificially inflate cost of equity estimates derived from the

5. Bond Yield Risk Premium 
The Company also proposed using the bond yield plus risk premium (BYPRP) 
model for determining ROE.  Ex. UI-AEB-1, pp. 33–37.  The BYPRP approach “is based 
on the fundamental principle that equity investors bear the residual risk associated with 
equity ownership and therefore require a premium over the return they would have earned 
as bondholders.”  Id.  The Company states that “because returns to equity holders have 
greater risk than returns to bondholders, equity holders require a higher return for that 
incremental risk.”  Id.  Further, the Company explains that “the risk premium approach 
estimates the cost of equity as the sum of the equity risk premium and the yield on a 
particular class of bonds.”  Id.

The Company developed the BYPRP model by regressing authorized ROEs for 
electric utilities to the US Treasury yield and adding risk premium.  Woolridge PFT, p. 88.  
OCC maintains several reasons why this approach is flawed.  First, it is a gauge of 
Commission behavior and not investor behavior.  Id.  Second, this approach “produces 
inflated measures of the risk premium because it uses historic authorized ROEs and 
Treasury yields, and the resulting risk premium is applied to projected Treasury Yields.”  
Id., p. 89.  Third, utility stocks have been selling above book value for the last decade, so 
OCC claims authorized ROEs are above what investors require, and the rate cases used 
in the Company’s analysis include vertically integrated electric utilities that have averages 
that are 30 to 40 basis points above distribution companies such as UI.  Id. 
The Authority reaffirms its determination that the BYPRP approach is not widely 
accepted today in utility ratemaking as this benchmarking-comparison methodology has 
been replaced by market-based approaches, such as DCF or CAPM. 
The Authority most recently rejected the BYPRP approach in the 2023 Aquarion 
Rate Case Decision.  At that time, the Authority reconsidered the risk premium plus 
approaches that used Commission-allowed ROEs as inputs and found the methodology 
was highly dependent on the number of companies included in the proxy group and the 
time period covered.  22-07-01 Decision, pp. 52–53.  The Authority further found that the 
approach was not a measure of investors’ market-based required returns but an 
assessment of prior regulatory commission behavior.  Id.  Consequently, since no 
evidence or rationale has been offered to the contrary, the Authority will continue to reject 
any approach using commission-allowed ROEs as the input data, including the BYPRP 
model. 
6. Comparable Allowed ROEs 
Although the Authority will not consider financial models based on other public 
utility commission allowed ROEs, the Authority will examine the ROEs approved in other 
jurisdictions.  Notably, the authorized ROE is supposed to reflect the economic and 
financial conditions expected during the Rate Year.  Previously allowed ROEs are, by their 
nature, not based on the most current financial data and generally provide a historical 
snapshot only.  Because allowed ROEs from other jurisdictions are historical and do not 
necessarily reflect current market conditions, the Authority finds that such allowed ROEs 
are limited to serving only as a point of reference. 
To that end, the Authority reviewed data on authorized ROEs nationwide compiled 
by Regulatory Research Associates (RRA).  RRA provides electric utility ROE data 
disaggregated by, among other things, case type (e.g., all cases, general rate cases, 
limited issue riders, etc.), by utility type (e.g., vertically integrated, distribution only), and 
by resolution (e.g., settled or fully litigated cases).

decisions issued by state and public utility commissions, the average authorized returns 
on electric and gas authorized returns rose slightly in 2024.  Interrog. Resp RRU-188 Att.

9.60% average in 2023.  Id.  For distribution-only rate cases, there was an increase in

b. Environmental, Social, and Governance Scores 
When determining an appropriate ROE, the Authority considers a utility’s 
environmental, social, and governance (ESG) score in assessing the utility’s risk profile.  
An ESG score measures how well a company addresses risk with respect to 
environmental, social, and governance issues.  “ESG scores can be used by investors to 
gain a better understanding of a company's long-term potential for value creation as it 
considers material non-financial impacts that could provide risks or opportunities to the 
company.”  Interrog. Resp. RRU-389, p. 1. 
A higher ESG score generally indicates a lower long-term business risk profile 
because it reflects stronger risk management and alignment with regulatory, 
environmental, and social expectations.  Conversely, a lower ESG score may suggest 
higher exposure to regulatory, reputational, or operational risk, resulting in a higher risk 
profile.

influence.  Similarly, Fitch assigned ESG credit relevance scores of 3.  Interrog. Resp. 
RRU-389, Att. 2, p. 3.  According to the Fitch report, a “score of '3' means ESG issues are

9. Approved ROE 
In determining a reasonable ROE, the Authority considers the analytical models 
for commensurate utility returns, allowed ROEs in other jurisdictions, the prevailing 
market conditions, and the Company’s risk profile.  The Authority considers the two 
analytical models (DCF and CAPM) to provide a target range for commensurate ROEs.  
The Authority generally weighs the DCF model results more heavily than the CAPM 
results because the DCF model relies on directly observable proxy company market data 
and provides a better measure of the COE for similarly situated utilities.  Conversely, the 
CAPM relies primarily on risk-premium studies and market predictions, which are more 
subjective in nature. 
Here, the DCF model as applied to the Authority Proxy Group indicates an ROE 
range of 8.70% to 9.60%, with a mean of 9.25% and a median of 9.16%.  The CAPM 
model produced an ROE range of 8.05% to 9.86%, with a mean of 9.067%. 
Given this range, the Authority must determine an ROE such that the Company 
has an opportunity to “cover . . . [its] capital costs, to attract needed capital and to maintain 
[its] financial integrity.”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  This statutory standard reflects 
the long-standing principle that “the return to the equity owner should be commensurate 
with returns on investments in other enterprises having corresponding risks and should 
also be sufficient to assure confidence in the financial integrity of the enterprise, so as to 
maintain its credit and to attract capital.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public 
Utility Control, 216 Conn. at 634–35.  In determining an ROE, the Authority “is not bound 
to the use of any single formula or combination of formulae” but again must balance 
“investor and consumer interests” and make “pragmatic adjustments.”  Woodbury Water 
Co., 174 Conn. at 264. 
Cognizant of this legal framework, the Authority has analyzed a wide array of 
considerations in reaching a determination, including, without limitation, the Company’s 
capital structure, its financial condition, ROEs from other jurisdictions, analytical models 
of commensurate returns, prevailing and anticipated market conditions, risk factors, and 
the regulatory environment. 
In brief, the Company is financially stable, maintaining an A- Rating from S&P, 
Baa1 from Moody’s, and A- from Fitch.  The Company is a subsidiary of AVANGRID, Inc.

10. Reductions to ROE 
a. Introduction 
The approved ROE is based on a similarly situated electric utility providing expert, 
efficient, and prudent management of the utility franchise; therefore, the Authority must 
consider whether to adjust the ROE for the Company’s actual management of its 
franchise.  As discussed in detail below, the Authority concludes that a cumulative twenty 
(20) basis point reduction to the Company’s allowed ROE is necessary to reflect the 
Company’s deficient performance in managing certain parts of its utility franchise and to 
incentivize the Company to improve its performance.  The interrelationship between 
investor returns and utility performance is well-established.  Importantly, the “rate-making 
process . . . involves a balancing of the investor and the consumer interests.”  Hope, 320 
U.S. at 603.  Similarly, a utility’s rate of return should be “reasonably sufficient to assure 
confidence in the financial soundness of the utility and should be adequate, under efficient 
and economical management, to maintain and support its credit and enable it to raise the 
money necessary for the proper discharge of its public duties.”  Bluefield, 262 U.S. at 
692-93 (emphasis added). 
Indeed, courts interpreting the “under efficient and economical management” 
language in Bluefield have determined that a utility’s rate of return may be adjusted to 
account for imprudent and inefficient management.  In re Citizens Utilities Co., 171 Vt. 
447, 460-61 (2000) (“Like Vermont, most other jurisdictions now accept the general 
principle that rates may be adjusted depending on the adequacy of the utility's service 
and the efficiency of its management.”); D.C. Transit System, Inc. v. Washington 
Metropolitan Area Transit Comm., 466 F.2d 394, 423 (D.C. Cir. 1972) (“We believe the 
constitutionality of governmental recognition of the interrelationship between fair return 
and quality service can hardly be doubted today.”); see also Richard J. Pierce & Emest 
Gellhorn, Regulated Industries in a Nutshell, pp. 134–135 (3d ed. 1994) (“The phrase 
‘under efficient and economical management’ [in Bluefield] is an important qualification.  
If an agency finds that a firm is not being managed efficiently and economically, it can 
lower the firm's allowed rate of return below the level otherwise required to meet the 
comparable risk test.”). 
Specific to UI, “[b]ecause § 16-19e(a) explicitly authorizes PURA to consider UI’s 
managerial expertise, its ability to meet its public responsibilities, and the prudency with 
which UI manages Connecticut’s natural environment, this court concludes that PURA 
has discretion to consider UI’s [performance] when determining UI’s authorized ROE.”  
March 13, 2025 Superior Court Decision, pp. 9–11. 
In Connecticut, the statutes governing rates reflect this important balance.  On one 
hand, “the level and structure of rates [must] be sufficient, but no more than sufficient, to 
allow public service companies to cover their operating costs including, but not limited to,

Docket No. 24-10-04 
 
Page 82 
 
appropriate staffing levels, and capital costs, to attract needed capital and to maintain 
their financial integrity, . . .”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  On the other, the Company 
has an affirmative obligation to be “technically, financially[,] and managerially expert and 
efficient,” and must perform its “public responsibilities with economy [and] efficiency” and 
rates must “reflect prudent and efficient management of the franchise.”  General Statutes 
§ 16-19e(a)(2), (3), and (5).  This constitutional and statutory balance is the foundation of 
the so-called “regulatory compact” between regulators and investor-owned utilities.  In a 
quid pro quo, the utilities are entitled to recover operating expenses and reasonable return 
on capital, and ratepayers, in exchange, are entitled to expert, efficient, and prudent 
management. 
Consequently, if a utility fails to uphold its end of the bargain by not providing 
expert, efficient, and prudent management, the regulator must adjust the scales to 
maintain the balance required by Hope, Bluefield, and General Statutes § 16-19e(a).  
Hope, 320 U.S. at 603; Bluefield, 262 U.S. at 692-93.  One way to accomplish this 
rebalancing is to reduce a utility’s allowed ROE.  See, e.g., Decision, December 17, 2014, 
Docket No. 14-05-06, Application by The Connecticut Light and Power Company to 
Amend Rate Schedules, p. 152 (ordering a 15 basis point ROE reduction for deficient 
storm response); Decision, April 27, 2011, Docket No. 10-09-08, Application of United 
Water Connecticut, Inc. to Amend Rate Schedules, p. 83 (ordering a 50 basis point ROE 
reduction for imprudent management of accounting, record keeping, and billing methods). 
An ROE adjustment is not a penalty for a specific act; rather, it serves as a 
mechanism to set rates commensurate with the level of service the ratepayers are 
receiving and, more generally, with the company’s adherence to its broader public 
responsibilities.  See In re Citizens Utilities Co., 171 Vt. 447, 454 (2000) (“the purpose of 
a rate-of-return reduction is not to penalize a company for specific acts of misconduct, but 
rather to set reasonable rates in cases where the consumers are not being adequately 
served due to inefficiency or improvidence or other like reasons.”). 
In this proceeding, the Authority identified several areas in which the Company’s 
performance did not reflect expert, efficient, and prudent management.  Importantly, some 
are not new.  The Authority and the Parties engaged in a robust discovery process, 
culminating in days of hearings, the filing of late filed exhibits and subsequent late filed 
exhibit hearings, post-hearing briefs and reply briefs.  Evidence from this lengthy 
adjudicatory process led the Authority to conclude that a reduction to the Company’s 
allowed ROE is warranted so that rates reflect the level of service and performance of the 
Company.

the Authority is also required to consider “the company's compliance with state law, 
regulations and the decisions and policies of the authority and the Department of Energy 
and Environmental Protection.  General Statutes §16-19gg(b)(2)(emphasis added).  
While the Company cites the correct legal standard for assessing the prudence of a public 
service company’s actions and expenditures, a prudency determination is neither the 
exclusive nor dispositive analysis in establishing an appropriate rate of return. 
The Authority’s broad regulatory authority and discretion allow it to set rates, 
including rates of return, based on consideration of any of its statutorily required 
considerations, or any combination thereof.  See Hope, 320 U.S. 591 (1944) (holding that 
what matters from a Constitutional perspective is the end result, not the analysis used to 
derive it); see also Barasch, 488 U.S. 299, 310 (1989) (affirming the holding in Hope that 
“[i]f the total effect of the rate order cannot be said to be unreasonable, judicial inquiry . . 
. is at an end.”); Woodbury Water Co., 174 Conn. at 264 (1978) (quoting Federal Power 
Commission v. Natural Gas Pipeline Co., 315 U.S. 575, 586 (1942)) (the Constitution 
does not bind the Authority “to the use of any single formula or combination of formulae 
in determining rates,” and the ratemaking process may involve “pragmatic adjustments.”); 
March 13, 2025 Superior Court Decision, p. 27 (articulating the Authority’s broad 
regulatory authority and discretion in the related context of allowing or disallowing the 
recovery of specific costs in rates). 
The protracted timeline on which the remediation of English Station continues to 
proceed, and the company’s failure to direct more of its resources (including the balance 
of its original $30 million commitment) to expediting the remediation effort, constitutes 
inefficient management.  Accordingly, a continued ROE reduction is warranted to provide 
continued incentivization for a more efficient and expedient completion of the Company’s 
remediation responsibilities as contemplated by the Merger Decision.

The AMI Decision established, inter alia, the structure and requirements for a 
Benefit Cost Analysis (BCA) to be included in each EDC’s AMI Plan.  AMI Decision, pp. 
22–25.  The primary goal of AMI deployment is to identify and realize the full spectrum of 
benefits from AMI.  Id., p. 11.  Simply acknowledging the potential benefits and assuming 
that they will be realized is insufficient.  Id.  Consequently, the Authority specified a 
detailed BCA framework with the aim of monitoring actual costs and the realization of AMI 
benefits. 
The BCA framework requires tracking metrics for a minimum of fifteen quantified 
benefits and at least six categories of costs.  Id., App. A, App. B.  Appendices A and B of 
the AMI Decision outline the benefit and cost categories and the targets and metrics that 
capture the availability and the realization of benefits.  Id.  For example, reduced meter 
reading costs are an AMI benefit.  AMI Decision, App. A, p. 1.  The number and percent 
of meters read via AMI monthly are metrics that capture the availability of the benefit.  Id.  
Monthly expenses and capital costs to support AMR meter reading (based on a historical 
average) and actual monthly expenses and capital costs to support AMI meter reading 
activities are metrics that capture the realization of this benefit.  Id.  Additionally, the 
calculation of benefits and costs is required to span a 20-year timeframe.  AMI Decision, 
pp. 14, 18. 
The Authority ordered the development of a BCA scorecard to standardize the 
tracking of the AMI benefit metrics and to assist with an ongoing evaluation of whether 
AMI investments are providing service to customers.  The Authority approved the 
scorecard template via motion ruling on September 18, 2024.  See Motion No. 32 Ruling, 
Docket No. 17-12-03RE02.  However, a crucial input to the BCA scorecard and a required 
element of the AMI Plan is the initial BCA calculation and the establishment of benefit

included in each EDC’s Final AMI Plan with respect to each identified AMI benefit: 
(1) Benefit Type and Description; 
(2) List and Description of All Necessary AMI Infrastructure and O&M Costs 
 Necessary to Unlock the Benefit; 
(3) Benefit Calculation Methodology and Establishment of a Benefit Target; 
(4) Annual Benefit Calculation; 
(5) Data to Track the Availability of the Benefit; and 
(6) Data to Track Benefit Realization.

iii. Due Process 
UI asserts that its due process rights have been violated because the Company 
was not put on notice that the Authority was considering a ROE reduction based on its 
AMI Plan (and other issues) 52 and because no party or intervenor in the proceeding 
advocated for an ROE reduction with respect to the Company’s AMI plan.  UI Exceptions, 
p. 80, n.59.  UI is conflating the notice that due process requires with respect to an 
opportunity to be meaningfully heard on substantive issues under consideration, see 
generally Burton v. Connecticut Siting Council, 161 Conn. App. 329, 341 n.12 (2015) ("A 
fundamental principle of due process is that each party has the right to receive notice of 
a hearing, and the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful 
manner”), with the Authority’s broad regulatory authority and discretion in setting just and 
reasonable rates.  See Hope, 320 U.S. 591 (1944); see also Barasch, 488 U.S. 299 
(1989); Woodbury Water Co., 174 Conn. 258 (1978). 
Here, the substantive matter under consideration is UI’s AMI Plan and its required 
Benefits-Cost Analysis (BCA).  The Company submitted its plan with its rate application 
in this proceeding.  See Ex. UI-CIP-1, p. 39 (“The Company’s Final AMI Plan, required in 
PURA’s Decision dated January 3, 2024 in Docket No. 17-12-03RE02, is being presented 
as Exhibit UI-CIP-8”); Ex. UI-CIP-8.  The Authority then requested clarifying information 
on various costs and benefits associated with AMI, which, per the Authority’s prior orders, 
should have been included in UI’s Final Plan and BCA.  See, e.g., Interrog. RSR-255, 
Interrog. RSR-256, Interrog. Interrog. RSR-258, Interrog. RSR-259, Interrog. RSR-260, 
Interrog. RSR-261, Interrog. RSR-262, Interrog. RSR-263, Interrog. RSR-264, and 
Interrog. RSR-265.  Moreover, the Authority expressly asked UI why certain costs were 
not included in the BCA portion of the Company’s Final AMI Plan.  Interrog. RSR-259. 
Thus, the Company was on notice that its AMI Plan was under review.  See Kinsey 
v. World PAC, 152 Conn. App. 116, 132 (2014) (noting, in the context of an administrative 
workers compensation proceeding, “a party may be apprised that a given claim is at issue 
by other means [than formal pleadings], such as the statements of parties at trial, the 
evidence they have introduced, or the papers they have filed....”)

2. Inflation Adjustment 
The Company proposes to escalate a number of Test Year expenses using an 
inflation adjustment factor of 8.15%, resulting in a pro forma expense of $4,505,562.  Late 
Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2, Sch. WP C-3.0, p. 2; Sch. WP C-3.19, p. 3 (Updated).  The Authority 
finds that escalating a Test Year expense by a generic inflation rate does not satisfy the 
requirement that a pro forma adjustment be known and measurable. In certain 
circumstances, the escalation of specific costs by an inflation rate may meet the known 
and measurable standard; however, such an escalation would require an evidentiary 
showing that the rate and its application constitutes a reasonable known and measurable 
change. 
Applying a broad index inflation factor to specific Test Year expenses is the 
exception rather than the rule because it is an imprecise methodology and not necessarily 
predicative of the Company’s actual Rate Year costs.  Indeed, such a methodology 
permits a utility to cherry-pick which expenses are escalated by inflation and which are 
escalated by other known and measurable changes.  With a utility incentivized to project 
higher expenses, this methodology likely results in broad-based inflation serving as the 
floor for expense escalation, thereby creating further upward pressure on rates. 
In the present case, the Company applied a generic inflation factor to 13 of the 18 
categories of O&M expenses for which it seeks recovery.  Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2 Supp., 
Sch. WP C-3.0.  In most instances, the Company failed to demonstrate that the use of a 
generic inflation adjustment constitutes a reasonable known and measurable change.  In 
fact, the Company often utilized a generic inflation factor when there were contracts that 
set forth pricing terms in the Rate Year, failed to utilize a more specific and reasonable 
methodology to project its Rate Year expenses, proposed inflation adjustments when the 
historical data it submitted suggested that the expenses had not increased with the rate 
of inflation, or otherwise made little attempt to explain historical expense trends and why 
the application of a generic inflation adjustment was reasonable.  While the Authority 
largely disallows the Company’s proposed generic inflation adjustments, it examines each 
of the inflated O&M expenses on a case-by-case basis and, in some instances,  
notwithstanding the Company’s failure to provide evidence to support various inflation 
adjustments, the Authority exercises its discretion and permits the Company to adjust 
certain Test Year expenses using an inflation rate.

be deferred for recovery in a storm regulatory asset.  13-01-19 Decision, pp. 33–34.  In

p. 152.  Accordingly, beginning in 2023, the Authority set the major storm threshold for 
charging storms to the reserve at $1.43 million.  Id., p. 153.  The Authority directed UI to 
apply the Handy-Whitman index on an ongoing basis with each biannual release of the 
index on January 1 and July 1, to update its major storm threshold each January 1 and

Whitman Index when it next requests recovery of major storm costs in the storm reserve.

To determine whether the Company’s requested compensation expenses for five

whether the Company, having not retained the additional staffing during the Test Year or 
Interim Period, has now demonstrated that additional staffing is a known and measurable

the proposed staff are purportedly necessary in the Rate Year, such staffing levels were 
likely necessary during the Test Year, if not during the Interim Period.  Accordingly, the 
actual costs for necessary staffing should be reflected in the Test Year and Interim Period.

services that might come to fruition during the Rate Year on a speculative basis.  A mere 
goal to hire more staff is not a known and measurable adjustment.

The Company’s and OCC’s respective arguments highlight the dilemma the 
Authority faces in determining whether the Company’s APA Plan should be recoverable 
from ratepayers.  On one hand, the Authority is charged with ensuring that rates are 
sufficient, but no more than sufficient, to allow the Company to support adequate staffing 
levels.  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  Thus, disallowing non-executive compensation 
in its entirety may result in below market compensation for the Company’s employees.  
Conversely, the Authority must also set rates that reflect prudent and efficient 
management of the franchise operation.  General Statues § 16-19e(a)(5).  As OCC 
highlights, various objectives tied to the APA Plan benefit shareholders rather than 
ratepayers, and certain ostensibly ratepayer-focused objectives should be improved to 
better serve ratepayer needs.  Moreover, there is only anecdotal evidence in the record 
that the program truly incentivizes employees, particularly if 100% of eligible employees 
receive employee incentive compensation.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-294; Interrog. Resp. 
OCC-299. 
Thus, in balancing the interests of ratepayers and shareholders, the Authority 
concludes that at least a portion of the Company’s objectives in the APA Plan are 
shareholder focused and do not otherwise represent prudent and efficient management 
of the franchise operation.  Indeed, by the Company’s own admission, 38.5% of its APA 
Plan goals are focused on shareholder or other interests, while the remaining 61.5% of 
its goals are focused on customer interests.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-137, Att. 1.  
Consequently, the Authority allows the Company to recover 61.5%, or $1,554 per 
employee, in non-executive incentive compensation to balance the interests of ratepayers

ii. Performance Metrics 
The Authority is required in a rate case to “consider the implementation of financial 
performance-based incentives and penalties and performance-based metrics.”  General 
Statutes § 16-19a(b).  Additionally, in exercising its discretion regarding whether to allow 
the recovery through rates of any portion of the compensation package for executives or 
officers or of any portion of any incentive compensation for employees of an electric 
distribution company, the Authority must consider whether to require that any such 
compensation recoverable through rates be dependent upon the achievement of 
performance targets.  General Statutes § 16-19yy.  If the Authority approves such 
performance-based incentives and penalties for a particular company, PURA is required 
to include it in the framework for periodic monitoring and review of the company’s 
performance pursuant to metrics developed by the Authority.  General Statutes § 16- 
19a(b).  Based on the record of this proceeding, the Authority continues to find it 
appropriate and necessary to tie a portion of executive compensation to performance 
metrics to provide the executives of UI and its parent companies with greater 
accountability to customers.  Moreover, as discussed below, the Authority finds it 
necessary to adjust or alter the previous performance metrics set forth in the 22-08-08 
Decision.  Indeed, the Company has continued to show, by aligning no more than 25% of 
its executive incentive compensation, which is funded through revenue requirements, with 
metrics that benefit customers, that its executive compensation program does not 
prioritize accountability to customers.  While the Company certainly bears responsibility 
to the investors who provide it with capital, the Company must be similarly responsible to 
the customers who provide it with revenue, and the Authority is empowered to make 
“pragmatic adjustments” that ensure a balance between investor and consumer interests.  
Woodbury Water Co., 174 Conn. at 264. 
The Authority previously directed the Company to follow three performance metrics 
in order to earn the full revenue requirement request for executive compensation.  The 
three performance metrics were: (1) Low-income customer identification metric; (2) 
Comprehensive and accurate customer communications metric; and (3) Payment 
arrangements for medical protection customers metric.  Parties have suggested that the 
performance metrics set forth in the 22-08-08 Decision be adjusted or altered for a variety 
of reasons. 
Regarding the low-income customer identification and payment arrangements for 
medical protection customers metric, the Company submitted evidence detailing its 
successful completion of each metric, while explaining that successful completion of the 
comprehensive and accurate customer communications metric was beyond the control 
of the Company.  UI Order No. 26 Compliance, Jan. 15, 2025, Docket No. 22-08-08.  OCC 
explained that due to the legally-required data sharing with the Department of Social 
Services (DSS), the low-income customer identification metric is no longer relevant.  OCC 
Brief, p. 80.  Similarly, OCC asserted that due to DSS data-sharing, the payment 
arrangements for medical protection customers metric has been affected and should be 
modified.  Id., p. 81.  OCC states that many medical protection customers are identified 
by DSS and should be excluded from this metric, thus measuring only medical protection 
customers without a financial hardship.  Id.  Regarding the comprehensive and accurate

The Company contends that its senior most executives provide “leadership,

Comprehensive and Accurate Customer Communications Metric: The 
Company shall measure comprehensive and accurate customer communications 
by counting the number of calls reviewed by the Company’s internal audit (IA) team

in relation to the percent of accurate and comprehensive calls in the Historical 
Period (denominator).  For additional guidance on this metric’s calculation 
methodology, see the Authority’s Rulings on Motion Nos. 81 and 87 (Motion No.

(2) 
Overall Arrears Metric: The purpose of this metric is to quantify the extent 
to which UI has reduced overall arrearages in each category (Category) as follows: 
residential hardship; residential non-hardship; and small business accounts.  The 
Company shall calculate the average number of accounts in arrears monthly.  The 
average number of accounts in arrears monthly in the Historical Period (numerator) 
will be divided by the average number of accounts in arrears monthly in the Current 
Year (denominator). 
(3) 
Successful Arrears Payments Metric: The purpose of this metric is to 
quantify the extent to which UI accomplishes the goal of reducing overall 
arrearages by helping customers on a payment arrangement successfully 
complete their payment arrangement.  UI shall calculate the average number of 
accounts that leave a payment arrangement without successful completion in 
relation to the total number of customers in a payment arrangement monthly.  The 
average monthly number of accounts leaving a payment arrangement without 
successful completion in the Historical Period (numerator) will be divided by the 
average monthly number of accounts leaving a payment arrangement without 
successful completion in the Current Year (denominator).

b. Pension 
The Authority permits the Company to recover a total of $9,502,832 in pension 
deferral expenses over a three-year period for a Rate Year amortization expense of

The Company reported a pension deferral balance of $13,053,936 as of August 
2023.  Ex. UI-RRP-22A, pp. 1–2. However, the Authority previously permitted the 
Company to recover a pension deferral of $12,880,858, which included an approved 
pension cost of $11,226,758 and carrying costs of $1,654,100.  22-08-08 Decision, p. 
191; Ex. UI-RRP-22d, p. 3.  The Company explained that the Authority’s approval of the 
$12,880,858 deferred pension expense in the 22-08-08 Decision was for amounts 
accrued as of June 30, 2022.  Ex. UI-RRP-1, p. 85.  Thus, the Company’s $13,053,936 
pension deferral balance as of August 2023 consisted of $11,226,758, the remaining 
balance of the amortized pension costs approved in the 22-08-08 Decision and 
$1,827,178 in incremental pension costs incurred between July 1, 2022, and August 
2023.  Ex. UI-RRP-22d. 
Through the close of the Interim Period, the Company reported a $6,767,774 
deferral balance for pension expense approved in the 22-08-08 Decision, and $1,853,470 
in additional pension expense, which consists of the Company’s $1,827,178 incremental 
pension costs plus $26,292 in carrying charges.  Late Filed Ex. 1, Att. 2 Supp., Sch. WP 
C- 3.21, p. 1. 
The Authority previously explained that a regulatory asset for ratemaking purposes 
arises only after the Authority has scrutinized a deferred expense for consistency with 
General Statutes § 16-19e(a) and authorized recovery via an order in a rate proceeding.  
22-08-08 Decision, p. 27.  Additionally, the Authority further stated that carrying charges 
are not permissible on deferred expenses without prior Authority approval, noting, among 
other things, that allowing carrying charges to accrue on deferred expenses that have not 
been subject to scrutiny and prudence review is inconsistent with general ratemaking 
principles.  Id., p. 28.  Conversely, however, the Authority concluded that carrying charges 
are permissible on regulatory assets during the recovery period.  Id.  Specifically, when a 
deferred expense is deemed prudent, it becomes a ratemaking regulatory asset that is 
amortized over a period of time, and the Company may include carrying charges to 
compensate the Company for the time it will take to fully recover the regulatory asset from 
ratepayers.  Id., pp. 28-29. 
In the present case, while the Authority scrutinized and subsequently approved a 
$12,880,858 regulatory asset for pension expenses, which included carrying charges 
during the recovery period, the Authority did not do so for the $1,827,178 in pension 
expenses accrued after the 22-08-08 Decision.  As such, the Authority did not approve or 
permit the Company to treat its newly accumulated pension expense as a regulatory asset 
that accrues carrying charges.  As such, the Authority does not permit the Company to 
recover $26,292 in carrying charges it claims to have accrued in the intervening years.  
Nevertheless, the Authority will permit the Company to accrue carrying charges on the 
$1,827,178 incremental pension balance going forward because the Authority is 
authorizing the Company to treat the expense as a regulatory asset in the Rate Year.
