(h) Storm Deferral Refund Carrying Charge Adjustment 
In calculating the Storm Deferral Refund balance, the Company included carrying 
charges on the monthly net balance of storm deferral expenses, storm accrual, and 
mutual aid reimbursements.  Interrog. Resp. EOE-249 Supp. 2, Att. 2, p. 2.  The Company 
also stops recording monthly storm reserve accruals as of December 2024, and further, 
stops the balance as of September 31, 2025.  Id.  The Authority adjusts each of these 
items as set forth below. 
The Authority finds that UI improperly calculated carrying charges on a monthly 
basis based on the net of deferred expenses and the storm reserve accrual.  See Ex. UI-
RRP-22C, p. 2.  The Authority previously determined that carrying costs on deferred 
expenses are not permissible without explicit prior Authority approval, and allowing

Docket No. 24-10-04 
 
Page 177 
 
carrying charges to accrue on deferred expenses that have not yet been subject to a 
prudence review is inconsistent with general ratemaking principles.  22-08-08 Decision, 
p. 28.  That said, carrying charges should apply to the reserve accrual, which the 
Company collects from ratepayers as an offset to storm costs.  The reserve is the 
equivalent of a prefunded ratepayer loan (or the equivalent of a reduction to rate base), 
therefore it should accrue the applicable carrying costs (i.e., WACC) on amounts that 
have been collected from customers.  This finding is consistent with Authority findings in 
prior rate cases where reserves funded by ratepayers created to pay future claims are 
essentially regulatory liabilities and should therefore accrue carrying charges.  See 23-
11-02 CNG Decision, p. 40; 23-11-02 SCG Decision, p. 49.  Therefore, the Authority 
disallows the Company’s calculation of a credit of $80,343 of carrying charges through 
September 31, 2025, since it was calculated from the net of deferred expenses and the 
reserve accrual.  The Authority recalculates the Storm Deferral Refund balance to include 
carrying charges on the storm reserve, but to exclude the application of carrying charges 
on deferred expenses and mutual aid reimbursements. 
The Authority does this by calculating the storm accrual balance separately from 
the storm cost balance.  The resulting carrying charge balance as calculated on a monthly 
basis on the reserve accrual balance from August 2022 through October 2025 is a credit 
of $374,911. 
When calculating the storm accrual balance, the Authority also continues recording 
monthly storm accruals through October 31, 2025, which is the start of the Rate Year (the 
Company stops recording storm accruals as of December 2024).  Therefore, the storm 
accrual balance as of October 31, 2025, including carrying charges, is a credit of 
$4,708,244, which is shown in Table 62, below.

DEPRECIATION EXPENSE 
A depreciation rate study proposes annual depreciation rates to be applied to plant-
in-service balances.  The product of the depreciation rate and corresponding plant 
balance is the annual depreciation expense, which is a charge to a company’s operating 
expense reflecting the annual recovery or amortization of previously expended capital 
investment.  While depreciation expense is a function of both the depreciation rate and 
the related plant balance, this section focuses only on the Authority’s rationale for 
adjusting the Company’s proposed depreciation rates.  The Authority’s determinations 
related to the Company’s plant balances are described in Section IV.B, Plant-In-Service, 
above. 
UI seeks to use the depreciation rates approved by the Authority in the Company’s 
previous rate amendment proceeding.  Ex. UI-RRP-1, p. 81.  The Company asserts that, 
“[g]iven the short passage of time since” the Company’s prior rate case, the previously 
approved rates “remain reasonably applicable” and would eliminate the added expense 
of conducting a depreciation study.  Id.  Depreciation studies rely heavily on historical 
data, and studies generally do not provide new information if sufficient time has not 
passed to change the historical data.  Application, Ex. UI-RRP-27, p. 1.  Depreciation 
studies should be conducted approximately every three to five years.  Id.  Neither OCC 
nor any other party contested the proposed depreciation rates.  The Authority approves 
the Company’s proposed depreciation rates as shown in Table 65, below.

VIII. 
RATE DESIGN 
A. 
LEGAL STANDARD 
The Authority is statutorily charged with regulating the rates of Connecticut’s public 
service companies and UI is a public service company within the meaning of General 
Statutes § 16-1.  General Statutes § 16-19.  Consequently, UI must “file any proposed 
amendment of its existing rates with the [A]uthority.”  General Statutes § 16-19(a).  Once 
a proposed amendment has been filed, the Authority: 
[s]hall make such investigation of such proposed amendment of rates as is 
necessary to determine whether such rates conform to the principles and 
guidelines set forth in section 16-19e, or are unreasonably discriminatory or 
more or less than just, reasonable, and adequate, or that the service 
furnished by the company is inadequate to or in excess of public necessity 
and convenience . . . . 
General Statutes § 16-19(a). 
Rate design objectives include: (1) the approval of cost-based just, and reasonable 
rates that promote further equalization of rates across the Company’s divisions; and (2) 
revenue stability.  See General Statutes § 16-19e(a). 
In striking this balance and making pragmatic adjustments, the Authority is guided 
by General Statutes § 16-19e(a), which states, in relevant part, that the Authority shall 
examine proposed rates in accordance with the following principles: 
(4) that the level and structure of rates be sufficient, but no more than 
sufficient, to allow public service companies to cover their operating costs 
including, but not limited to, appropriate staffing levels, and capital costs, to 
attract needed capital and to maintain their financial integrity, and yet 
provide appropriate protection to the relevant public interests, both existing 
and foreseeable . . . [and] (5) that the level and structure of rates charged 
customers shall reflect prudent and efficient management of the franchise 
operation. 
In furtherance of this statutory framework, the Authority typically employs the rule 
of cost causation, which allocates costs to customers and cost categories based on the 
costs they cause a utility to incur.  The Authority also generally attempts to equalize class 
rates of return, as such practice ensures that rates are not unreasonably discriminatory, 
while balancing the regulatory philosophy of gradualism to, among other reasons, avoid 
customer rate shock.  See J Lazar et al., Electricity Regulation in the US: A Guide (2d Ed. 
2016), p. 67, available at https://www.raponline.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/rap-
lazar-electricity-regulation-US-june-2016.pdf (“sudden large rate changes should be 
avoided where possible to avoid undue new burdens on some classes of customers”).  
Consistent with the philosophy of gradualism, the Authority typically requires rate class 
revenue reductions or increases to be within one and one quarter times the overall 
distribution revenue increase.  See 16-06-04 Decision, p. 108; see also 13-01-19

Decision, p. 153.  Finally, the Authority considers whether “existing or future rate 
structures place an undue burden upon those persons of [low-income] status” as 
contemplated by General Statutes § 16-19e(b).  The Authority weighs the above 
principles and considerations in determining appropriate cost and revenue allocation 
approaches and rate designs.

The Company filed an allocated cost-of-service study (ACOSS) based on the

The Company’s proposed ACOSS utilizes the Minimum System Study (MSS) approach

costs associated with AMI infrastructure were classified using the labor allocator, which

Although the Authority acknowledges OCC’s concerns with the MSS approach, it 
is not clear that the basic customer method is a superior alternative.  Costs classified as 
demand-related under the basic customer method, such as poles and conductors, are 
unaffected by changes in demand.  Both the Company and OCC acknowledge that these 
costs are primarily driven by the geographic dispersion of customers (i.e., circuit miles).  
Rates Panel Rebuttal PFT, p. 12; Palmer Surrebuttal Test., Mar. 24, 2025, p. 3.  
Unfortunately, geographic dispersion does not offer a clear billing determinant.  As such, 
the Authority accepts the premise that the number of customers is an acceptable, if 
imperfect, proxy for costs unrelated to demand, and that the MSS approach is an 
appropriate method for categorizing these costs in this proceeding.  Primary distribution 
infrastructure has both demand- and customer-related components.  Rates Panel 
Rebuttal, p. 12.  Even in a hypothetical sense, there can be no minimum-sized system 
that contains only secondary distribution while meeting any non de minimis level of 
demand.  Therefore, the reasoning supporting the use of the MSS approach extends to 
both primary and secondary distribution plant.  The Authority affirms the Company’s 
proposed classification of AMI meters as 100% customer-related, which is consistent with 
cost causation principles, as argued by CIEC. 
The MSS approach is a just and reasonable approach to cost classification, but 
the minimum system’s load-carrying capacity should be considered when allocating 
residual demand-related costs.  The Company did not consider the minimum system’s 
load-carrying capacity because customers benefit equally from minimum system costs 
since “all customers impose some lowest common denominator amount of minimum load 
on the system.”  Rates Panel Rebuttal PFT, pp. 11–12; Late Filed Ex. 83.  All customers 
benefit equally from the minimum system, and this benefit can be quantified, although the 
Company did not attempt to do this.  See Hr’g Tr., 1328:19.  Specifically, each customer 
should be allocated an equal share of the load-carrying capacity affiliated with the 
hypothetical minimum system, applied towards the relevant demand allocators.

Authority determines that it is appropriate to use the Company’s load-carrying capacity

71, Att. 4.  Specifically, in the Company’s adjusted ACOSS model, the Company applied 
the adjustment only for line transformers and conductors (overhead and underground).  
Id.  Although the Company did not explain this choice, the Authority assumes that a similar

In evaluating the Company’s rate design proposal, the Authority must consider how 
to best balance the goals of providing a strong signal to shift load to off-peak periods with 
generally accepted rate design principles of gradualism, customer acceptance, and 
understandability.  The Company has not provided sufficient justification for allocating 
substation- and feeder-related demand costs to the on- and off-peak and seasonal 
periods based on the percentage of substations and feeders peaking in those periods.  
The Company’s approach may be appropriate to guide cost allocation but should not be 
used without modification, as it implies that there are no substation- or feeder-related 
demand costs associated with serving load outside the hour when that substation or 
feeder peaks. 
As UI acknowledges, rate design is an art and a science, yet the Company’s 
approach to allocating substation- and feeder-related demand costs attempts to make the 
exercise purely quantitative.  Ex. UI-RP-1, p. 11.  Rates should be set according to both 
cost causation and empirical research into appropriate price differentials that can be 
reasonably expected to induce customer behavioral change without unduly penalizing 
customers.  Although the Company conducted a thorough analysis to determine 
appropriate timing of on-peak periods in its end-state rates, the price differential in the 
proposed near-term rates is concerning.  Setting a large price differential without 
changing the on-peak window (currently eight consecutive hours, from 12:00 to 8:00 p.m.) 
may dissuade enrollments and penalize customers currently enrolled on Rate RT that 
would not have a reasonable opportunity to shift their demand away from the on-peak 
period.  Equally concerning is that an average customer enrolled on Rate R will save 
money by enrolling on Rate RT without changing their consumption patterns.  Interrog. 
Resp. RRU-172, Att. 1, p. 2; Hr’g Tr., 1347:9–11.  This implies that if all residential

all underlying costs would remain identical.  This reality also may help explain the 
Company’s conclusion that customers transitioning from Rate R to Rate RT did not 
change their consumption behavior; existing rates provide little impetus to change 
behavior if the average customer can save money by doing nothing.  See Hr’g Tr., 
1464:20–1465:16.  The proposed rates, therefore, may create both bill shock and free-
ridership problems for customers.  The Authority is particularly concerned that the high 
price differential will have the opposite result from that intended by causing a net reduction 
in enrollment on Rate RT.

The Company indicated that its customers prefer opt-in rates, based on a survey 
conducted in 2024.  Interrog. Resp. RRU-176.  The importance of opt-out rates is not 
based solely on consumer preference; rather it is grounded in cost causation principles 
and long-term affordability.  Customers must face cost-reflective price signals to make 
informed decisions about their electricity consumption, which will lead to efficient 
investments in the distribution system.  Masking true price signals with flat volumetric 
rates does not protect ratepayers and only ensures that underlying time-varying costs are 
recovered inefficiently.  It is concerning that the proposed end-state rates have almost no 
price differential between the winter on-peak and off-peak periods.  Behavioral change is 
difficult and will not happen instantly.  For many customers, the transition to opt-out TOU 
rates will be the first time they are exposed to the concept that the cost of electricity varies 
by the time of day.  As customers become familiar with TOU rates, it is important for rates 
to induce behavior changes during hours that drive costs both today and in the future.  In 
light of the projected transition to a winter-peaking grid in the state and region, providing 
a muted winter price differential risks reinforcing undesirable behaviors.

In sum, the record indicates that the Company’s preparation and progress towards 
implementing opt-out TOU rates have been inadequate.  The Company acknowledged 
that it has not developed a detailed customer education plan, attributing this to the fact 
that the details of such a plan are dependent on when opt-out TOU rates will become 
effective.  Rates Panel Rebuttal PFT, p. 27.  The information presented by the Company 
in Exhibit UI-CSP-1 lacks important details, including the timing of the transition, proven 
consumer protection mechanisms such as shadow billing and bill stabilization, and a 
specific plan for low-income discount rate (LIDR) customers.  The Company testified that

1. Revenue Decoupling Mechanism 
The Authority approves the revenue elements included herein to be included as 
“other revenues” for purposes of the Company’s Revenue Decoupling Mechanism (RDM) 
calculation. 
Generally, an EDC may only charge rates that have been approved by the 
Authority in a general rate proceeding under General Statutes § 16-19.  However, the 
General Assembly established several statutory schemes that allow the EDCs to recover 
specific costs through adjustment mechanisms, including the RDM.  General Statutes § 
16-19tt.  The Authority conducts an annual proceeding to determine rates for the various 
adjustment mechanisms.  Specific to the RDM, the Authority adjusts the Company’s 
actual distribution revenues to its allowed distribution revenues and orders an adjustment 
to rates to reflect any over- or under-recovery captured in the RDM during the Company’s 
annual rate adjustment mechanism (RAM) proceeding.  General Statutes § 16-19tt.  The 
Authority has defined the term “allowed distribution revenues” as used in General Statutes 
§ 16-19tt to refer to the EDC’s annual revenue requirement as approved by the Authority 
in its most recent distribution rate case pursuant to General Statutes § 16-19(a).  Decision, 
Jan. 29, 2025, Docket No. 22-01-04, PURA Annual Review of the Rate Adjustment 
Mechanisms of the United Illuminating Company, p. 6.  Additionally, the Authority defines

Docket No. 24-10-04

“actual distribution revenues” as all revenues realized during the course of the Company’s 
distribution business in a calendar year, with the exception that revenues accounted for 
or reconciled through another established mechanism are excluded from the RDM 
calculation.  Decision, Jan. 29, 2025, Docket No. 22-01-04, PURA Annual Review of the 
Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of the United Illuminating Company, p. 9. 
During a distribution rate case, the Authority sets the Company’s annual revenue

2. Earnings Sharing Mechanism 
The Company proposes that its earnings sharing mechanism (ESM) continue as it 
is currently constructed with two adjustments: (1) the ESM calculation should reflect UI’s 
actual equity ratio, not its authorized equity ratio; and (2) the ESM should not exclude

Docket No. 24-10-04 
 
Page 218 
 
disallowed expenses.  Ex. UI-RRP-1, p. 131.  The Authority declines to adjust the 
calculation of the ESM as the Company proposes and instead directs the Company to 
continue calculating the ESM with a 50/50 split between ratepayers and shareholders 
from the first dollar of over-earnings above the allowed ROE calculated on a calendar 
year basis. 
The Authority rejects the Company’s proposals on the same basis articulated in 
the Company’s last rate case.  22-08-08 Decision, pp. 220-221.  First, adjusting the ESM 
such that it reflects the Company’s actual equity ratio subverts the Authority’s 
determination of what constitutes a reasonable capital structure for ratemaking purposes.  
Indeed, as demonstrated in Section V.C.3., Capital Structure Analysis, the Authority 
undergoes a vigorous exercise to set an appropriate ratemaking capital structure that 
weighs several factors while balancing both investor and consumer interests.  The 
Company’s proposal unsettles the balancing of such interests by adjusting the point at 
which a 50/50 split of earnings is executed to the benefit or detriment of shareholders or 
consumers, depending on the Company’s actual capital structure. 
Second, including disallowed expenses in the ESM as the Company proposes 
distorts the delineation between revenue collected from ratepayers through rates and the 
Company’s earnings.  The Authority applies the legal principles articulated in Section II, 
Standard of Review to determine the Company’s revenue requirement.  Thus, disallowed 
expenses have been deemed not to meet the legal requirements necessary to be 
included in base distribution rates.  Importantly, the Authority in approving a revenue 
requirement is not mandating the Company to cease all expenditures not included in the 
revenue requirement; rather, the Company can elect to continue paying for disallowed 
costs from its earnings after any overearnings are appropriately allocated to ratepayers 
in accordance with the ESM.  In other words, disallowed expenses should not be included 
in the ESM calculation to determine the Company’s earnings subject to a 50/50 split; they 
are elective expenses the Company may pay for out of its own earnings. 
Accordingly, the Authority directs the Company to continue calculating the ESM 
with a 50/50 split between ratepayers and shareholders from the first dollar of over-
earnings above the allowed ROE calculated on a calendar year basis as set forth in the 
22-08-08 Decision.

ii. Unified Pole Rate Formula 
After determining that a single rate should be used for all attachers, the Authority 
must consider how that rate should be calculated.  The FCC formula for cable and telecom 
attachers differs only in how the “space factor” is determined.  The space factor is 
intended to account for the space of a utility pole that the attachment uses, and it is then 
multiplied by the other factors of the FCC formula to assign costs to attachers based on 
that useable space.  See Ex. UI-RP-10, p. 1.  The formula utilizes the pole costs (initial 
pole and installation costs, ongoing maintenance costs, etc.) and assigns an estimate of 
those costs to each attacher based on the space the attacher uses on the pole.  22-08-
08 Decision, p. 262. 
The cable formula for determining usable space is the simpler, taking the average 
pole height in feet (from UI records) and subtracting 24 feet, the “unusable space” of a 
utility pole (a constant value established by the FCC). 131  See Ex. UI-RP-10, pp. 1–2.  UI’s 
poles average 39.49 feet, leaving usable space of 15.49 feet (39.49 - 24).  Cable 
attachments are assumed to use 1 foot of space on the pole, so the space factor of 6.46% 
is determined by dividing 1 foot of cable space by 15.49 feet of total usable space (1 / 
15.49).  Id., p. 2.  Accordingly, 6.46% of the costs allocable to attachers (as determined 
by the FCC formula) are assigned to each attacher because that is the estimated space 
used by each attacher. 
The telecom formula is slightly more complex, because it adds back a portion of 
the 24 feet of “unusable space.”  Ex. UI-RP-10, p. 1.  The telecom formula space factor 
begins by assigning each attacher 1 foot of usable space, just as the cable formula does.  
Ex. UI-RP-10, p. 1.  The telecom formula then divides two-thirds of the 24 feet of unusable 
space among 5 attachers (a number predetermined by the FCC) presumed to be sharing 
the pole ((2 / 3)x(24 / 5) = 3.2).  Id.  The portions of usable space and unusable space are 
added, and that sum is divided by 39.49 feet, the total average pole size, to arrive at a 
space factor of 10.64% ((1 + 3.2) / 39.49 = 10.64%).  Id.  The telecom formula then 
reduces the space factor by 0.66 to arrive at 7.02% (10.64% x 0.66).  Id. 
Both cable and telecom attachments are subject to National Electric Safety Code 
(NESC) clearance requirements that require the cables to maintain a minimum height 
above roadways.  Interrog. Resp. RSR-317.  Because the 24-foot clearance requirements 
are required for all attachers, the inclusion of a portion of the unusable space into the pole 
attachment formula properly reflects that attachers require that portion of the pole to 
provide service and is commensurate with its use.  Applying the telecom rate to cable 
attachers will not harm those attachers nor inhibit broadband expansion or service

Id.  The program evaluates performance based on three equally weighted metrics: SAIDI, 
SAIFI, and Safety, each accounting for 33.33%.  Id.  In 2023, union employees met the 
SAIDI and Safety targets but did not meet the SAIFI target, resulting in a payout of 
$141,281.  Id.  While these metrics, particularly SAIDI and SAIFI, are tied to system 
reliability, and Safety is a core operational value, they are not explicitly aligned with 
broader ESG objectives. Therefore, the Authority finds limited evidence that ESG 
performance influences union compensation in a measurable or intentional manner. 
The Authority directs the Company to strengthen transparency regarding the 
influence of ESG objectives on compensation across all employee levels.  This includes 
clarifying how ESG-related expectations are defined, communicated, and measured, 
particularly at the operating company level.  The Authority directs the Company to report 
on the role of ESG goals with employee compensation and employee incentive 
compensation in its next rate case application.

c. Environmental Justice Communities 
Avangrid outlines its equity strategy through the Just Transition framework in its 
2023 Sustainability Report.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-31, p. 1.  The Company asserts that the 
strategy focuses on four stakeholder groups—customers, communities, workforce, and 
suppliers, with the goal of minimizing negative impacts and enabling positive outcomes 
as the Company transitions to a clean energy economy.  Id.  Avangrid’s Board periodically 
reviews corporate policies that support these objectives, including commitments to health 
and safety, human rights, people management, and stakeholder engagement.  Id.  The 
Company indicates that these policies guide its equity approach and are publicly available 
on its corporate governance webpage.  Id. 
For each stakeholder group, Avangrid identifies core principles and related 
implementation strategies.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-31, p. 1.  For customers and 
communities, these strategies include promoting equitable access to energy 
technologies, providing usage and affordability tools, supporting economic development, 
and ensuring proactive communication around capital projects.  Id.  For workforce and 
suppliers, strategies include upskilling, local workforce development, supplier adaptability 
support, and expanding opportunities for equal opportunity suppliers.  Interrog. Resp. 
UPA-31, p. 2. 
At the operating company level, UI states that its Community Relations personnel 
engage all 17 municipalities in its service territory and maintain a presence in

enrollment events, typically in partnership with local nonprofit organizations.  Id.  UI also 
participates in several Connecticut programs that target low-income and distressed 
municipalities.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-18.  These programs include: 
(1) The Community Partnership Initiative, which promotes participation in energy 
efficiency programs; 
(2) The Neighborhood Assistance Act Tax Credit Program, which supports 
nonprofit-led energy initiatives;

4. ESG Conclusion 
OCC raises significant concerns regarding the lack of operating company-level 
ESG governance, transparency, and accountability at UI.  OCC Brief, p. 45.  OCC 
highlights that, although Avangrid promotes robust corporate ESG commitments, UI has 
not demonstrated local implementation, oversight structures, or measurable outcomes.  
Id., p. 46.  OCC also emphasizes that Connecticut ratepayers—not shareholders—fund 
100% of UI’s ESG contributions, despite Avangrid benefiting from investor confidence tied 
to ESG positioning.  Id.  In OCC’s view, these deficiencies directly undermine the 
Company’s request for a higher return on equity.  Id. 
The Authority agrees and finds that Avangrid has not established sufficient 
operating company-level ESG governance structures, targets, or oversight mechanisms 
at UI, despite its stated extensive corporate sustainability commitments.  Throughout this 
proceeding, the Company consistently acknowledged that ESG responsibilities and 
performance tracking reside exclusively at the corporate level.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-15; 
Interrog. Resp. UPA-26.  UI employees do not hold defined sustainability responsibilities 
or incentives, nor does the utility maintain utility-specific metrics to track ESG 
implementation.  H’rg Tr., 475:16–22. 
Although the Company points to Avangrid’s Just Transition framework and 
participation in several Connecticut-based programs, such as the Community Partnership 
Initiative, Energy Storage Solutions, Residential Renewable Energy Solutions, and the

Docket No. 24-10-04 
 
Page 252 
 
CT EV Charging Program, the Company has not demonstrated how UI evaluates its 
equity or sustainability impact within these programs, nor how stakeholder input shapes 
program delivery or outcomes.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-31; Hr’g Tr., 474–476.  Without utility-
level performance indicators or internal accountability mechanisms, UI cannot show 
whether these initiatives are effectively reaching environmental justice communities or 
driving measurable ESG progress. 
Furthermore, UI is not in alignment with Avangrid’s gender diversity commitments.  
While Avangrid’s public ESG goals include increasing the representation of women in 
senior leadership to 40% by 2025, UI did not reference this target in any ESG-related 
interrogatory responses.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-35.  As of 2023 and 2024, no women held 
senior leadership roles at UI.  Late Filed Ex. 19, Att. 1.  Additionally, the Company 
confirmed that it does not formally measure the effectiveness of internal advancement or 
succession planning strategies designed to support women or other underrepresented 
groups.  Hr’g Tr., 495:12–22. 
This disconnect between public ESG claims and operating company-level 
execution reflects a shortcoming in implementing Avangrid’s ESG priorities in 
Connecticut.  While the Company’s 2022-2023 sustainability reports frame Avangrid as a 
leader in ESG transparency, its Connecticut operations did not demonstrate operating 
company-specific contributions, oversight, or measurable outcomes.  In addition, UI’s 
contributions to Avangrid’s ESG performance—through programs that advance 
environmental and social goals—are funded by Connecticut ratepayers. 
The Company has also linked its continued participation in clean energy initiatives 
to an increase in its allowed return on equity, indicating that its support for these programs 
is contingent upon cost recovery certainty rather than embedded in its long-term strategy.  
Hr’g Tr., p. 1760:22–25; 1761:1–9.  This includes statements suggesting that the current 
earned return is insufficient to sustain participation and that modernization investments 
may be deferred until the Company earns a higher return.  Ex. UI-RPP-1, p. 34–35.  This 
disconnect between Avangrid’s public ESG positioning and UI’s local implementation 
reflects a failure to translate corporate commitments into operating company-level 
accountability, transparency, or measurable outcomes.  While Avangrid has emphasized 
the reputational and financial advantages of its ESG positioning, those benefits are not 
shared equitably between shareholders and ratepayers. 
As such, the Authority finds that improvement in the Company’s ESG governance 
is needed to ensure UI ratepayers and local operations tangibly benefit from Avangrid’s 
ESG goals and actions.  Despite repeated claims of leadership in sustainability and 
corporate responsibility, the Company has made no meaningful effort to operationalize 
those commitments at the operating company level.  The Authority finds this disconnect—
between stated values and on-the-ground execution—both troubling and inconsistent 
with the public positioning the Company has chosen to promote.  As such, in the 
Company’s next rate amendment application, the Company shall report ESG metrics 
demonstrating its contributions to Avangrid’s ESG performance as discussed herein.  
Such reporting serves as a targeted performance signal to reinforce the expectation that 
ESG related claims—particularly those used to bolster public image or attract investor

interest—must be matched by transparent action, measurable results, and equitable cost 
sharing at the operating company level.  Failure to demonstrate operating company-level 
contributions to Avangrid’s ESG goals could warrant a potential downward adjustment to 
the Company’s authorized ROE in a future proceeding.  Such an outcome would serve 
as a targeted performance signal of the expectation that ESG participation, particularly

The Company asserts that the Authority oversteps by imposing ESG-related 
directives that are inconsistent with UI’s corporate discretion.  UI Exceptions, p. 88 (citing 
Missouri ex rel. Southwestern Bell Telephone Co. v. Public Service Commission of 
Missouri, 262 U.S. 276, 289 (1923)). UI claims that the Authority is effectively 
micromanaging the Company by requiring the Company to make business decisions 
based on PURA’s judgment and not that of the Company’s management.  UI Exceptions, 
p. 158.  However, the Authority’s directives are narrowly focused on operating company-
level reporting and accountability, not on substituting business judgment or mandating 
expenditures.  Consistent with the Authority’s statutory obligations to ensure 
transparency, just and reasonable rates, and alignment with public interest goals under 
General Statutes §§ 16-19e and 16-244i(d), enhanced local ESG reporting is necessary 
to assess the prudency of cost recovery, the effectiveness of implementing ESG 
initiatives, and the proportionality of shareholder versus ratepayer benefits.  Moreover, 
the record reflects the Company’s own admissions regarding the absence of defined ESG 
responsibilities, performance metrics, and governance structures at the operating 
company level—facts that support narrowly tailored reporting requirements.  See Interrog. 
Resp. UPA-15; Interrog. Resp. UPA-26; Interrog. Resp.UPA-40; Interrog. Resp. UPA-41; 
Hr’g Tr., 475:16–22. 
Finally, the Company’s assertion that Avangrid may eliminate UI-specific ESG 
contributions does not demonstrate that such contributions are integral to the Company’s 
long-term strategy or embedded within its sustainability values, but it suggests that they 
are discretionary and contingent on favorable regulatory outcomes.  See UI Exceptions, 
p. 159.  Such actions would undermine Avangrid’s public ESG commitments and result in 
inconsistent and unsubstantiated local implementation.  Enhanced transparency 
requirements are necessary, and any potential future ROE adjustment may depend on 
the level of operating company integration, local implementation, and broader ESG 
outcomes.  Participation in programs that advance the public interest should not depend 
on earnings enhancements but should reflect the Company’s core obligations and 
sustained accountability to the communities it serves.
